title: Calculator with Error Handling
story: You're building a command-line calculator for a school project. The user types expressions like 'ADD 5 3' and expects the answer. But what if they type 'DIV 10 0' or 'MUL x y'? Instead of crashing with a cryptic error, your calculator returns a clear message explaining what went wrong.
why: Parsing operator strings and operands into a calculator teaches command dispatch with pattern matching and numeric parsing with error propagation — the foundation of every interpreter.
analogy: This calculator is like a fast-food order taker. You say 'BURGER 2 COKE 1' — the taker splits your words, checks that 'BURGER' and 'COKE' are valid menu items, verifies the quantities are actual numbers, and only then rings up your total. If you say 'PIZZA asdf' — the taker says 'Sorry, PIZZA isn't on the menu' rather than charging you $asdf.
try_it: Add MOD (modulo — check b != 0) and POW (power — multiply a by itself b times using a loop). Then add NEG (negate a, ignore b) and ABS (absolute value of a). What happens when someone types 'DIV 10 two'? Does your error message tell them which operand is bad? Improve the error message to say 'First operand is not a number' vs 'Second operand is not a number'.
tips: Parse operands BEFORE the operator dispatch — if parsing fails, don't bother checking which operator was used
Division by zero is a special case that requires a guard BEFORE the actual division
The `?` operator on `string.str_to_int` auto-converts parse errors — but you lose the ability to say WHICH operand failed
common_mistakes: Checking the operator before parsing operands — you might reject the operator when the real problem is a bad number
Using `?` for division by zero — `b == 0` is a domain error, not a parse error; handle it explicitly
Forgetting string indices are zero-based when splitting — the second space is at position `space2`, not `space1 + space2`
